title: Quartiles, Quantiles & Interquartile Range — Cheat Sheet

sections.definition: Values that split a sorted dataset into four groups of equal size.

key_values.name: Q1 (First Quartile)
key_values.description: Value below which 25% of the data falls. Also the 25th percentile.

key_values.name: Q2 (Second Quartile)
key_values.description: The median. Value below which 50% of the data falls. Also the 50th percentile.

key_values.name: Q3 (Third Quartile)
key_values.description: Value below which 75% of the data falls. Also the 75th percentile.

manual_calculation_steps: Sort the dataset from smallest to largest.
Find Q2 (the median) of the full dataset.
For odd n: Q2 is the middle value. For even n: Q2 is the average of the two middle values.
Method 1 (exclusive): Q1 = median of all points BELOW Q2. Q3 = median of all points ABOVE Q2.
Method 2 (inclusive): Q1 = median of all points ≤ Q2 (including Q2). Q3 = median of all points ≥ Q2 (including Q2).
sections.important_note: There is no universally agreed-upon method for calculating quartiles. Different tools may report slightly different values, especially for small datasets.

sections.definition: The minimum, Q1, Q2 (median), Q3, and maximum of a dataset. Provides a quick overview of range, centrality, and spread.
sections.visualization: Displayed in a box plot: the box spans Q1 to Q3 (length = IQR), with a line at the median.

sections.definition: Values that split a dataset into groups of equal size. n-quantiles produce n+1 groups using n-1 cut points.
sections.key_relationship: n quantiles → n groups → (n−1) cut points. Wait, correction: n-quantiles split data into n groups, requiring (n−1) cut points. Actually: if you have n-quantiles, you get n groups and (n−1) dividing values.
sections.correction: More precisely: 'n-quantiles' refers to n−1 cut points that divide data into n equal groups. E.g., quartiles = 3 cut points → 4 groups.

r_examples.returns: Value separating the first 23% from the rest (23rd percentile)

notes: The quantile() function does NOT require the dataset to be pre-sorted.
Single-value calls (e.g., 0.23) technically return a percentile, not a true quantile set, but are still useful.
R supports 9 different quantile calculation types (Type 1–9); default is Type 7 (linear interpolation).

sections.definition: The difference between the third quartile (Q3) and the first quartile (Q1). Measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
sections.why_use_iqr: Unlike the range (max − min), the IQR is robust — outliers have little effect on it because it only depends on Q1 and Q3, which are positional statistics not influenced by extreme values.
sections.robust_statistic_definition: A statistic is 'robust' when outliers have little impact on its value.
sections.example: dataset_one = c(6, 9, 10, 45, 190, 200) → IQR = 144.5; dataset_two = c(6, 9, 10, 45, 190, 20000000) → IQR = 144.5 (identical despite massive outlier)

r_functions.description: Built-in function from the stats library. Returns IQR in one step.

sections.box_plot_connection: In a box plot, the box spans from Q1 to Q3. The length of the box equals the IQR.

pitfalls: Confusing the number of quantiles with the number of groups (n quantiles → n groups, n−1 cut points).
Using Q2 (the median) when calculating IQR — it's NOT needed. IQR = Q3 − Q1 only.
Forgetting to sort data when calculating quartiles by hand (R's quantile() handles this automatically).
Assuming there's only one 'correct' method for quartile calculation — multiple valid methods exist.
Mixing up quartiles (0.25, 0.5, 0.75) with quintiles (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) or deciles (0.1–0.9).
Confusing range (max − min, NOT robust) with IQR (Q3 − Q1, robust).
